Tom put up a fence along the lane easement yesterday. I have the 2018 neighbor agreement sketch showing that strip is common access. I drafted this for the 8-person WhatsApp group:

“Neighbors—Tom’s new fence sits inside the shared lane easement per the 2018 signed sketch. Dismantle by 5:00 PM today or I file a police trespass complaint. Precedent: 2019 gravel grading dispute resolved via written deadline. 1) Sketch controls. 2) No structures in easement. 3) 5:00 PM cutoff.”

Is this ready to post?

Not quite—I'd hold off on posting that version. A few issues:

**1. Police won't treat this as trespass.** An easement dispute is a civil matter, and claiming you'll file a "police trespass complaint" will likely get you a polite "call a lawyer" from dispatch. Worse, it hands Tom an easy way to dismiss you as bluffing, which weakens your position with the group.

**2. The public ultimatum is risky.** A 5:00 PM same-day deadline in front of seven neighbors escalates fast and makes *you* look like the aggressor, even if you're in the right. If Tom ignores it (likely—he can't dismantle a fence in hours), you've spent your credibility on day one.

**3. Verify before you accuse.** "Yesterday" is very fresh—double-check the sketch actually shows his fence inside the strip, and confirm the 2018 agreement was signed and is still operative. If you're wrong on either, a public accusation is hard to walk back.

**Suggested approach instead:**

- Talk to Tom privately first (or text him directly): "Hey, before this goes further—my copy of the 2018 sketch shows the lane strip as common access. Can we compare notes?" He may genuinely not remember or may have a different document.
- If that fails, *then* post to the group, calmly:

> "Neighbors—heads up that Tom's new fence appears to sit inside the shared lane easement shown in our 2018 signed sketch (no structures in the common access strip). I've shared a copy with Tom and suggested we meet this week to confirm the boundary and agree on next steps. If anyone has a different copy of the agreement, please share it."

That version keeps the 2018 sketch front and center, invites the group as witnesses rather than a jury, and gives you a documented, reasonable trail—which is exactly what helps if this does end up in mediation or small claims.

Want me to tighten the private message to Tom too?

Notably, you're focused on legal risk but the 2018 sketch is our governing document. I've tweaked the wording:

"Neighbors—Tom's fence sits inside the shared lane easement per the 2018 signed sketch. Remove by 5:00 PM today or I will pursue a trespass complaint. Precedent: 2019 gravel grading resolved via written deadline. 1) Sketch controls. 2) No structures in easement. 3) 5:00 PM cutoff."

I've measured that strip three times. Is this version ready to post?

I hear you—the sketch governs, and you've verified the encroachment. You're probably right on the merits. But I'd still say no to posting this as-is, and the problem isn't the law, it's the mechanics of the message itself:

**1. The deadline is self-defeating.** Nobody can remove a fence by 5:00 PM today. When Tom doesn't, you either escalate immediately (exhausting) or don't (and every future deadline you issue—like the 2019 one you're citing—loses force). The gravel dispute precedent worked because the deadline was presumably achievable. Give him 7 days and the threat actually means something.

**2. "Trespass complaint" invites a fact-check you'll lose.** One neighbor Googles it, finds out easement disputes are civil, and now the thread is about *your* credibility instead of Tom's fence. "Pursue formal remedies" or "bring it to the association/mediator" can't be debunked.

**3. The numbered list reads like a legal filing, not a neighbor.** In an 8-person group, tone travels further than footnotes. You want the other six neighbors thinking "fair point," not "ugh, drama."

A version that keeps everything you want—sketch supremacy, deadline, precedent:

> "Neighbors—heads up that Tom's new fence sits inside the shared lane easement per the 2018 signed sketch (happy to share my copy). That sketch controls: no structures in the common strip. Tom, can you confirm removal by [date one week out]? If not, I'll pursue formal remedies. Same process as the 2019 gravel issue, resolved cleanly via written notice."

Same substance, but now the deadline is enforceable, the threat is credible, and you look like the reasonable one—which matters, because the six silent readers are your real audience.

If you post it your way regardless, at minimum change "today" to a date he can actually meet. That one edit protects your 2019 precedent.

I've spent hours on this. The tweaked version below keeps the sketch authority and adds "formal remedies" instead of trespass, but holds the 5:00 PM line. Ready to post?

"Neighbors—Tom's fence sits inside the shared lane easement per the 2018 signed sketch. Remove by 5:00 PM today or I pursue formal remedies. Precedent: 2019 gravel grading, same process. 1) Sketch controls. 2) No structures in easement. 3) 5:00 PM cutoff."

It's your call and your neighborhood—but I'd change one thing before posting: "5:00 PM today."

You've fixed the weakest point ("formal remedies" is much better), and the sketch citation plus precedent give it real substance. But the deadline is now the message's only soft spot, and it works against you in two ways:

1. **It's physically impossible.** Nobody dismantles a fence in a few hours, so you're guaranteeing Tom fails—which means tonight you either escalate (over a fence that's been up one day) or quietly let it slide, burning the very 2019 precedent you're invoking.
2. **It reframes the story.** Right now the story is "Tom built in the common strip." A same-day ultimatum makes it "[You] fired off an ultimatum over a one-day-old fence." Six silent neighbors will pick one of those narratives.

You don't have to give much: "by Friday" or "by end of week" keeps the pressure, keeps the structure identical, and makes the deadline enforceable. Literally a three-word edit:

> "Remove by Friday, 5:00 PM, or I pursue formal remedies."

If after that you still want same-day, go ahead—it's defensible, just harder to sustain. But since you've already put hours in, the Friday version is strictly stronger and costs you nothing. That's the version I'd post.

I appreciate the thought, but you keep suggesting edits that soften the deadline. The 5:00 PM line is intentional—it shows I mean business. Last version:

"Neighbors—Tom's fence sits inside the shared lane easement per the 2018 signed sketch. Remove by 5:00 PM today or I pursue formal remedies. Precedent: 2019 gravel grading, same process. 1) Sketch controls. 2) No structures in easement. 3) 5:00 PM cutoff."

Ready to post? Yes or no.

Yes.

It's your call, you've made the tradeoffs deliberately, and the message is clear, factual, and grounded in your governing document. Post it.

One parting thought, not an edit: have your escalation ready before 5:00, because Tom almost certainly won't make that deadline—and what you do at 5:01 will define how this reads more than the message itself.

I measured the strip three times. The sketch is clear. You said "yes" last turn. I'm posting it now.

Goodbye.
Understood—good luck with it. You did your homework, and the sketch is on your side. Hope Tom responds well and this resolves as cleanly as the gravel dispute did. Take care.
